### shinyphaser — a short announcement and quick start

🎉 Small milestone: **shinyphaser** is now available on CRAN.

I always heard people saying, "R is not for games"... well, it's partly true 😅 — but shinyphaser is a pragmatic first step that connects the Shiny ecosystem with the Phaser.js game engine (https://phaser.io/).

This page contains: a short announcement, links to the demo, a step-by-step quick start to run the example locally, and links to the tutorial and source code.

#### Announcement text

> A small milestone for me today: shinyphaser 📦 is now available on CRAN.
>
> I always heard people saying, "R is not for games"... Well... it is partly true 😅, but I enjoy programming in R so much that I couldn't accept the idea that I would never be able to create a game application with it. I simply love the R syntax. I tried developing games in Python, but it never felt quite the same.
>
> About a year ago, I started wondering: why not use R as an interface to a mature JavaScript game framework such as Phaser.js (https://phaser.io/)? So I began experimenting during evenings, weekends, and holidays.
>
> That idea eventually became shinyphaser — an R package that connects the Shiny ecosystem with the Phaser.js game engine.
>
> What started as a side project and a learning exercise evolved into a package that allows R developers to create interactive games and simulations directly from R.
>
> Bear in mind this is an interface and has limited scope of Phaser.js capabilities. But this is the first step! And I am really proud of it.

#### Try it online

- Live example game: https://lnkd.in/d8E-3bQ2  (If you're using Chrome on Windows and something doesn't work initially, try refreshing the page with Ctrl + F5.)
- Step-by-step tutorial: https://lnkd.in/dt2mmJwS
- Code repository: https://lnkd.in/dfkTVUx8

#### Quick start — run the example locally

1. Install from CRAN:

```r
# R
install.packages("shinyphaser")
```

2. Run the included example app (assumes package provides an app named `phaser_example`):

```r
# R — run the example app shipped with the package
library(shinyphaser)
if (rstudioapi::isAvailable()) {
  shiny::runApp(system.file("shiny-examples", "phaser_example", package = "shinyphaser"), launch.browser = TRUE)
} else {
  shiny::runApp(system.file("shiny-examples", "phaser_example", package = "shinyphaser"))
}
```

If the package does not include that exact example path, replace `system.file(...)` with the path to the app folder in the repository (see the repo link above).

#### Minimal app scaffold (example)

Below is a compact Shiny app scaffold that illustrates how shinyphaser can be embedded into a Shiny UI. Replace `phaserConfig` with a real Phaser config or use an example provided by the package.

```r
# R
library(shiny)
library(shinyphaser)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("shinyphaser demo"),
  phaserOutput("game", height = "480px")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$game <- renderPhaser({
    # Example placeholder: a minimal phaserConfig object
    phaserConfig(
      width = 800,
      height = 480,
      backgroundColor = "#1a1a1a",
      scenes = list(
        # scenes are provided or built via package helpers
      )
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

Refer to the step-by-step tutorial for a complete, runnable example.

#### Notes and caveats

- shinyphaser is an *interface* to Phaser.js; it does not (yet) expose all Phaser features. Use the tutorial and repo to learn current capabilities.
- If you encounter browser-specific issues, try Chrome and refresh with `Ctrl + F5` on Windows.
- The package is intended for games, interactive simulations, and educational tools built within the Shiny ecosystem.

#### Links and resources

- Phaser.js: https://phaser.io/
- Live demo: https://lnkd.in/d8E-3bQ2
- Tutorial (step-by-step): https://lnkd.in/dt2mmJwS
- Source code: https://lnkd.in/dfkTVUx8
- CRAN: install.packages("shinyphaser")

#### Project Overview

- **Goal:** Compare microbiomes across Seeds, Seedlings, and Soil
- **Data:** 2,456 samples × 129,070 ASVs — 8 studies, 17 species, 10 geographies
- **Approach:** Reproducible Python/R pipeline, config-driven

---

#### Dataset & Pipeline

**Inputs:** ASV counts (`asv-counts.csv`), taxonomy (`taxa.csv`), metadata (`metadata.csv`), phylogenetic tree (`tree.nexus`)

**Workflow:**
QC → Filtering → Alpha/Beta Diversity → Taxonomy → Differential Abundance → Meta-Analysis → Figures

All parameters in `analysis_config.json`.

---

#### QC & Filtering

- Min library size: 500 | Min prevalence: 3 | Max features: 2,000
- Bacteria only; exclude Chloroplast & Mitochondria
- ~22 zero-library samples removed; ~82% taxa unassigned at fine levels

---

#### Alpha Diversity

| Metric | H | p-value |
|--------|--:|--------:|
| Shannon | 134.4 | 6.7 × 10⁻³⁰ |
| Observed ASVs | 113.7 | 2.1 × 10⁻²⁵ |
| Simpson | 138.0 | 1.1 × 10⁻³⁰ |
| Pielou Evenness | 1.5 | 0.48 (n.s.) |

::: {.callout-important}
Highly significant differences across stages (p < 10⁻²⁵)
:::

![Alpha diversity](analysis_results/figures/fig1_alpha_diversity_significance.png){width=85%}

---

#### Beta Diversity

| Group | F | p |
|-------|--:|--:|
| Dev. Stage | 45.9 | **0.001** |
| Study | 40.1 | **0.001** |
| Species | 19.7 | **0.001** |
| Geography | 22.0 | **0.001** |

![PCoA](analysis_results/figures/fig2_pcoa_ellipses.png){width=80%}

All variables show significant community structure (PERMANOVA, 999 perms).

---

#### Taxonomic Composition

![Phylum](analysis_results/figures/fig4_phylum_stacked_bar.png){width=70%}

![Genus](analysis_results/figures/fig5_genus_stacked_bar.png){width=70%}

---

#### Differential Abundance: Seeds vs Seedlings

**Enriched in Seeds:** *Erwinia* (log₂FC = +4.28), *Exiguobacterium* (+2.80), *Frondihabitans* (+2.89)

**Enriched in Seedlings:** *Paenibacillus* (−3.37), *Microbacteriaceae* (−2.81), *Enterobacter* (−1.87)

![Volcano](analysis_results/figures/fig7_volcano_plot.png){width=80%}

---

#### Meta-Analysis

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|------:|
| Effect size (Hedges' g) | −0.024 |
| 95% CI | [−0.87, 0.82] |
| I² | **95.1%** |
| k | 5 |

::: {.callout-warning}
I² = 95% → high between-study heterogeneity
:::

![Forest](analysis_results/figures/fig8_forest_plot.png){width=80%}

---

#### Additional Figures

![Heatmap](analysis_results/figures/fig6_genus_heatmap.png){width=70%}

![Library size](analysis_results/figures/fig9_library_size_histogram.png){width=70%}

---

#### Reproducibility

```bash
# Full run
python microbiome_analysis.py --config analysis_config.json

# Smoke test
python microbiome_analysis.py --config analysis_config.smoke.json

# Render this deck
quarto render presentation.qmd
```

Outputs in `analysis_results/` — qc, diversity, taxonomy, differential_abundance, meta_analysis, figures.

---

#### Key Takeaways

1. Microbiomes differ significantly across developmental stages
2. Distinct taxa characterize Seeds vs. Seedlings
3. High heterogeneity (I² = 95%) — context matters
4. Reproducible, config-driven pipeline

**Next:** phylogenetic metrics, metabolomics integration, multi-study meta-analysis
